newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danes expect Clinton visit to put them on the map.
newsitem.headline: Danes expect Clinton visit to put them on the map.

text.p: When U.S. President Bill Clinton arrives in Denmark on Friday for a brief visit he will find a country where he has no treaties to hammer out, no disputes to resolve and where nobody really cares about his sex life or party fund-raising activities.

To Copenhageners, finally enjoying a long-awaited summer and the start of the city's annual jazz festival, the Clinton visit is another entertainment event, although few expect him to play his saxophone.

Academics say that Denmark, a founder-member of NATO and a country where English is spoken widely and well, has a "little brother complex" toward the United States and longs to bask in the elder sibling's approval.
The Americans are certainly not holding back in dishing out an almost embarrassing amount of goodwill.
"The United States has no closer and more trusted friend in Europe, and perhaps the world, than Denmark," U.S. Ambassador Edward Elson, a friend of Clinton, told journalists this week.
He added an extra bonus for Danish pride, particularly regarding rivalry with neighbouring Sweden.
"It is the first time an incumbent U.S. president has ever been to Scandinavia and when he did it was to Denmark, to say thank you to a trusted friend," Elson gushed.
Danes out strolling in the city on Thursday had modest expectations of the visit.

"We are just a little pawn in world affairs, so I do not know how important the Clinton visit is. The most important thing is that Americans get to know where Denmark is, that Copenhagen is not the capital of the Netherlands," student teacher Michael Olsen told Reuters.

In the absence of any real political agenda, media attention for the past week has been focused on whether or not the public will need tickets to see Clinton give an open-air speech in the city's 17th century Nytorv (New Square) on Saturday.
The answer is no.
Tickets and security passes will be needed by journalists and official guests in special seating close to Clinton. No special documents are needed for the rest of the square.

There, where in 1756 two counterfeiters were the star turns at the country's last public execution, a jazz trio, pop-rock band and classical pianist will entertain an expected crowd of some 20,000 for two hours before the president speaks.
The event will be relayed on giant screens nearby and on live television.
That will, in fact, be the most that ordinary Danes see of Clinton before he boards Air Force One for the flight home to Washington, immediately following his 1330 GMT speech.

Arriving on Friday evening from Bucharest, he will helicopter directly from Copenhagen international airport to Queen Margrethe's summer palace at Fredensborg, about 30 km (20 miles) north of the capital.

He will spend the night and Saturday morning with the Queen and her family and have lunch at the palace before leaving to place a wreath at a memorial to those killed in World War Two in resistance against Nazi occupation.
A brief meeting with Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen follows before the public rally.
Not everyone in Denmark loves the Americans of course. It may be the land of Hans Christian Andersen but life today is not a fairy tale.

A total of 30 political parties, labour unions and groups such as Red Youth, the Danish-Cuban Association, the Hod-Carriers' Union, and the Iraqi Communist Party in Denmark are to demonstrate opposition to U.S. policy on just about everything.
Their protest march through the city will end a block away from the Clinton show at Nytorv, but only after the president has left the square.
